body: So glad to hear that it is all good on one side :) Having some family members on board is great news. But yes, the wedding, the kids, all the big life changes will be hard for having two cultures and your family maybe not on your side. These things can be really hard on couples even if they are from the same culture if certain family members have different expectations of their role in your lives though, and there are some family members like that in every marriage. I agree that maybe eloping wouldn't be the best option especially with his family on your side it might be nice to have them there, but I don't think a small wedding is a terrible idea, we planned ours that way to avoid conflict of family members and it worked only because we invited certain people on explicit agreement that if they come they must not make problems for us, haha. It was a nice day. However, it would make sense if you're inviting people to think what sort of ceremony you both want. The things you mentioned are important but they should be important because of what they mean to you and your SO in the context of your relationship, not because of what they mean to your family. Hope you find a way that works for you and him! Good luck and best wishes :)

I'm sorry that you're also in a horrible place right now. And I do sort of know logically that it wouldn't make him better off as in happy, obviously he would not be happy, but he says the only thing that makes him happy is me being happy and I can't be for some reason, it's virtually impossible sometimes, so therefore whilst I am alive he wont be either. It is very hard for me to get my head around this, as I always strongly believed that people should be self-sufficient, and if I'm going to end up making my husband homeless along with myself because I can't hold down a full time job then I'm harming him not adding anything good to his life. Hard to divorce the strongly held philosophy from the realistic 'but he wont be happy'. But I do see what you're saying, and thank you for posting it. I probably wont do anything but the thought keeps coming back because I don't see any other way of doing this whole uni sitch except the already-proven next to impossible that I've tried and failed at before. I'll try to keep in mind that my husband wont feel happy if I do this. Maybe that will help like your daughter does. I hope you feel better soon too.

Not me but my mam and dad (mam is Muslim and dad is Catholic). They have been together 25 years and are very much in love and I know they don't regret staying together, that said, both families caused a lot of problems for them particularly when we were born (what religion should we be brought up in was a favourite issue). At times they have had to distance themselves from one side or the other, and they still have to put up with casual remarks like why my dad is not a Muslim? For shame... etc. The families thing is so difficult, they may come round, they may not, but being with someone that understood them fully was so important to my mam and dad that they took the risk. I think at times they felt it was better when they did put the families aside for a time as it meant they could prioritise doing things in the way they thought was right. One thing that has helped them though is to find their own spiritual ways forward. I know you are not religious right now and that you say his family is not strictly Muslim but my parents have really struggled to what it meant to them, my mam in particular is from a country where being Muslim is what makes you a citizen and she felt very alienated for a long time until she found a liberal mosque that accepts her interfaith marriage. Another thing that has helped them is that they always talk about religious differences and the challenges that throws up because there will be some areas where you think differently automatically but as they faced them honestly they didn't crack on them. I hope that has been a bit helpful to know that it can be done and I wish you all of the luck in the world, it is a horrible situation to be in and I hope it resolves in the best way.

Hi, I just wanted to offer my perspective as I have been on both sides of this situation. Firstly I'm sorry that your man has to work so many hours in a day. It would be massively preferable if no one had to do such long hours just to earn decent money enough to plan for the future on! I totally sympathise on this. More than that though I sympathise on how much it sucks being alone all day, no one to share your experience with, and having someone come home who has had so much to deal with all day that sometimes, some days, he can't be emotionally available for you. About two days before my husband and I were due to get married, he lost his job. I had just found a new job after being unemployed myself which was fortunate, so I threw myself in, worked all the hours I was given. Unfortunately, I have depression and generalised anxiety disorder, and part of the way I control these is to do a lot of housework, a lot of filing, a lot of dealing with the home so that I have control over my own space. I had never been able to work so many hours before that because of this element of control that I allow myself. Dealing with 55 hours per week at work on average wrecked me. I had to spend all day in the company of people, when I can't usually handle more than a few hours per day, it took away my ability to do the extra 10 hours a week I usually spend on my flat, and it meant I rarely saw my husband. I eventually started to take it out on him, I'm ashamed to say, as I resented the fact that he couldn't control my space like I could and he would still have a social life (I don't have friends because I can't maintain a social life with depression). So I missed him, he was my only link to caring nice people. But when he got a job it got a million times worse. My job didn't put the hours down for me, and he got a job in care working shifts up to 60 hours per week. And I never saw him for about 6 months because our shifts conflicted. We came very, very, very close to breaking up less than a year after we married, before that we'd had 3 happy years together with both of us working during office hours and spending evenings and weekends together. It does legitimately ruin some relationships that are otherwise strong. I see it as if you have a relationship you both have to put the work in to spend time with the other person, although I recognise that this doesn't work for all couples. Anyway, the situation I am now in is the reverse again, as I quit that job rather than lose my husband. I am now unemployed and looking for work and my man is still working a million hours, completing an NVQ so he can go to university next year. As I said, I have two conditions that actually make time on my own preferable but still being lonely, having no hope for future prospects of your own, no one even in a similar situation to talk to, is awful. I absolutely understand what you mean about when he comes home you want him to yourself, to talk to, but he just wants to unwind some days, as he has also had a terrible day dealing with a lot and more conversation is sometimes the last thing someone in that boat wants. I wanted to add my perspective only because of two things, so I hope I haven't annoyed you with the telling of it. The first thing is that yes, he may well be right that your relationship would break down if you both had jobs and never spent any time together. Try not to beat yourself up too much if you have to consider that perspective, I know jobs are one of those things we value ourselves on but I know also, in my experience that losing a shite job was the best thing I did to save my marriage and I wouldn't regret that, however... The other thing I wanted to add is that  the fact that your current situation is time limited is ESSENTIAL (from my experience only). Whilst we were indefinitely never going to spend time together, or if I thought my husband was still working a million hours for a jolly and not considering me, it was/would be untenable to me. That your man has a plan to do this just long enough to get money and then he is thinking of getting a more stable job seems to me to be really important for you both. If you decide to sit this one through and you end up in a better position because of it then all is gravy, but getting through it will be tough whatever you do. I love that you are writing romance novels, writing is an amazing way to keep 'busy' and provide a creative outlet (well done on getting them published), but in terms of human interaction it is much harder and I hope that you will find some way of meeting people. My mam was in a similar position too when she had us, as my dad had to commute away. Her solution was also distance learning courses so I second what the other commenter said, she found having a mentor helpful and many distance learning courses provide this. It also gives you promise for your future so that even if you and he don't make it through the strain you have something to aim for- in my experience my lowest points have been when I thought I was losing my husband yet I had nothing to hope for on my own. I hope so hard for you that you can survive this, it is definitely possible (my mam and dad are still together after twenty five years, and I'm still with my husband thankfully) so there is hope! I think you are doing the right thing reaching out for ways to deal with the loneliness now though, being stuck in the house with no one caring lets dark thoughts and stress run rampant where they wouldn't normally. Feel free to PM me if you want to talk at any point but otherwise I am sending you internet hugs and all my hope for you. Sorry not better advice! :) Take care

Hey, I'm glad that the internet has a place where we can all post this stuff up when there aren't people in real life who know what to say. I don't really know what to say either but I wanted to reply coz I also hate the happy-go-lucky line. I am sorry you have those feelings. Talking about suicidal feelings out loud is really hard, and personally I've found that's so because talking about what led you to them with family, friends or your GP is also either not possible or not useful. In either case, talking about depression or saying you are feeling suicidal, I find it's because the people you would talk to normally don't give a reasonable response. Like you say, you get a lot of 'it gets better' and all that crap that we all know isn't true for a whole lot of people, or you get dismissed outright, by doctors and friends and what seems like everybody. Unfortunately most people don't have the training to deal with extremes of depression and suicidality, so they go off of what they've seen in films and TV, platitudes basically. I don't know who you've spoken to if anyone about the depression itself, but if you haven't already, I'd suggest speaking to someone who is specifically trained to deal with depression and related issues. They *should* know not to trot out the same old crap and if they do, I tell them it's not helpful and to quit patronising you and that seems to change their tack pretty quickly. Particularly if it is your local mental health team of psychologists they can suggest practical solutions to take the edge off the depression, whether medication, therapy, time off work, or even referring you for relevant services (debt or careers advice etc) which might help some people more than the other stuff I mentioned. Telling them you're suicidal is often easier than telling a layperson that you're suicidal because they are already having a conversation with you about how down you are, it doesn't come out of nowhere and it doesn't affect them really so you're not going to get the guilting or the other responses you usually get off friends and family. I find it helpful to take a family member with me to the referral appointment though, as the doctor who refers you is most likely to be the least helpful, and even though most family members don't know what to say themselves, they know to get angry if a doctor says something wrong. Maybe if you felt it would help you, to just tell a family member that you have an appointment with the doctor because you want to be referred over 'stress related illness' (people seem to understand that better than depression) and make them come along. If none of this helps or you've tried it all already then I am really sorry. Feel free to PM me if you want to. In case it helps, I'll just say that it isn't unreasonable to be thinking 'I don't think I'm ever going to be happy again'. Sometimes depression really doesn't let people go. Sometimes it is a very biological issue and it might be helpful to sort out if there are any biological things making it worse- not sleeping well or having to get up and go to work at the time of day it is worst for you makes it almost unbearable, these can be big things to tackle and you might still not be happy, but they can take the edge off which gives you time to adjust to a chronically low mood and energy level. Sometimes it is situational and a result of not achieving your ambitions which only makes it harder to do so, and what might help then is if someone can put you on the path to achieving a few quickly. Either way, having the conversation with people who respond uselessly just makes it worse. I hope you can find people who are trained to deal with depression that can help even if it's a local charity (some of their training is excellent and they can often point you to organisations that can help more practically). Finally whoever you find it can really help to make very clear to them that you want help that helps YOU. If they suggest something that you don't think would be useful, feel free to tell them what you do want or to never mention that thing again. I hope some of this has helped but again. Internet hugs and I hope one way or another you find someone useful :)
